c.tagline: Roman Tarraco on the Costa Daurada, ruins above the Mediterranean.

taxi.fareNote: Metered fares are standard; hail on the street or book a licensed taxi via Cabify or Free Now, as Uber is not active here.

emergency.note: 112 is the general EU-wide emergency number connecting to police, fire, and ambulance.

hood_landmark.El Miracle (Beachfront): Platja del Miracle beach amphitheatre Tarragona
hood_landmark.Part Alta: Tarragona Cathedral Part Alta old town
hood_landmark.Rambla Nova (Centre): Rambla Nova Balco del Mediterrani Tarragona

avoid.reason: Watch for pickpockets around Rambla Nova, the beaches and the train station in summer.

hood_desc: Tarragona's walled medieval old town layered over Roman Tarraco, home to the Gothic cathedral, the Praetorium, and steep stone lanes; the atmospheric heart for history and the must-see sights.
The city's grand tree-lined boulevard running down to the Balcó del Mediterrani viewpoint, lined with shops, cafes, and terraces; central, flat, and the easiest base for getting around.
The historic fishermen's quarter by the working port, famous for no-frills seafood restaurants and the daily fish auction; a salty, authentic spot for a long lunch away from the tourist core.
The in-town beach neighbourhood tucked below the Roman amphitheatre, with a broad sandy strand, seasonal chiringuitos, and sea-view hotels; a relaxed base for a beach-first stay.
A modern residential extension of shops, everyday eateries, and the bus station, well connected but short on sights; a practical, budget-friendly area for a longer or car-based stay.

water.note: Tap water is safe, though its chlorinated taste leads many to choose bottled.

transit.hours: EMT city buses run roughly 6:00 AM to 11:00 PM; night service is very limited, so taxis or ride apps cover late hours.
transit.note: Tarragona has no metro or tram; the EMT municipal bus network serves the city, while Renfe Rodalies and regional trains connect it to Barcelona, Reus and the Costa Daurada.
transit.pay: Pay the driver in cash on EMT buses (~€1.65) or use a rechargeable T-mobilitat / multi-trip card for cheaper fares; trains use separate Renfe tickets.

train: Renfe long-distance (Camp de Tarragona AVE station)

transit.m: Hispano Igualadina airport bus to Tarragona center (~30 min)

tip.r: Not expected; locals round up or leave small change, and 5-10% for good service in restaurants is generous.

food.name: Calcots amb romesco
food.desc: Sweet young onions charred black over vine cuttings, peeled by hand and dunked in romesco. A winter ritual eaten in bibs from January to March.

places.name: Masia Bou
places.note: The original calcotada masia in the town that invented them; huge grills and set menus.

places.name: Cal Ganxo
places.note: Country masia doing classic calcotades followed by grilled lamb and butifarra.

places.name: Barquet
places.note: Long-established Tarragona restaurant that runs calcot menus through the season.

food.name: Romesco de peix
food.desc: The mother sauce of the region, made from nyora peppers, almonds and hazelnuts, turned into a fisherman's stew with monkfish, potatoes and clams.

places.name: El Posit
places.note: Fishing-quarter restaurant working straight from the port auction next door.

places.name: Casa Guri
places.note: Family-run kitchen doing seasonal Catalan cooking with local fish at its heart.

places.name: Sol Ric
places.note: Refined Catalan institution with a garden terrace and strong fish cookery.

food.name: Arrossejat
food.desc: El Serrallo's own dish: short noodles or rice toasted dry then simmered in fish stock, served with a fierce bowl of allioli on the side.

places.name: Barquet
places.note: Best-known name in town for arrossejat and other Tarragona rice dishes.

places.name: El Posit
places.note: Quayside dining room in the fishermen's guild building; rices cooked to order.

places.name: La Caleta
places.note: Seafront restaurant built on port fish, with rices and fideua as the specialities.

food.name: Fideua
food.desc: Paella made with short noodles instead of rice, cooked in fish stock with cuttlefish and prawns until the tips stand up and crisp.

places.name: La Caleta
places.note: Named for its seafood fideua and lobster arros caldos, with sea views.

places.name: Casa Guri
places.note: Reliable fideua in the fishing quarter where locals eat on Sundays.

places.name: Barquet
places.note: Classic address for the full range of Tarragona rice and noodle dishes.

food.name: Xato
food.desc: Winter salad of curly endive with salt cod, tuna, anchovies and olives, bound in a nut-and-pepper xato sauce closely related to romesco.

places.name: Barquet
places.note: Traditional menus that bring out xato and other Catalan winter dishes in season.

places.name: Casa Guri
places.note: Mediterranean-rooted cooking with local seasonal salads and salt cod.

places.name: Mercat Central de Tarragona
places.note: Modernista market hall; buy the endive, cod and sauce to assemble xato yourself.

food.name: Suquet de peix
food.desc: Slow fisherman's stew of rockfish, potato and a picada of almonds and garlic, thickened until the broth clings to the spoon.

places.name: El Posit
places.note: Serrallo standard-bearer for suquet, cooked with whatever the boats landed.

places.name: Sol Ric
places.note: Elegant version of the stew in a long-running Tarragona restaurant.

places.name: La Caleta
places.note: Port-fresh fish and shellfish, including suquet and grilled sepietes with allioli.

food.name: Vermut
food.desc: Nearby Reus is Spain's vermouth capital, and the pre-lunch vermut with an olive and a siphon splash is a Tarragona weekend fixture.

places.name: Part Alta bars
places.note: Squares in the walled old town fill with vermut drinkers before Sunday lunch.

places.name: Mercat Central de Tarragona
places.note: Market bars pour vermut on tap with conservas from the stalls around them.

places.name: El Serrallo waterfront bars
places.note: Fishermen's quarter terraces where vermut comes with anchovies and crisps.

food.name: DO Tarragona and Priorat wine
food.desc: The province holds four wine appellations, from crisp whites and vermouth bases to the dark, mineral reds of Priorat and Montsant in the hills inland.

places.name: Sol Ric
places.note: Deep Catalan cellar to pair Priorat and Montsant reds with local fish and meat.

places.name: La Caleta
places.note: Local-leaning wine list built for seafood, with regional whites by the glass.

places.name: Part Alta bars
places.note: Small wine bars in the old town pouring Tarragona province bottles by the glass.

landmarks: Amfiteatre Romà (Roman Amphitheatre)
A 2nd-century arena carved into a seaside slope, where gladiators once fought against a shimmering Mediterranean backdrop that still frames Tarragona's most iconic photograph.
Tarragona Cathedral (Catedral de Santa Maria)
Crowning the old town's highest point, this fortress-like 12th-century cathedral blends Romanesque and Gothic styles around a serene sculpted cloister and treasure-filled diocesan museum.
Pont del Diable (Les Ferreres Aqueduct)
A remarkably intact Roman aqueduct spanning a pine-wooded valley outside town, its double tier of golden arches invites visitors to walk across the ancient water channel.
Balcó del Mediterrani
This palm-lined clifftop balustrade at the Rambla Nova's end delivers sweeping views over the amphitheatre, harbour and sea; touching its iron railing supposedly brings good luck.
Passeig Arqueològic (Roman Walls)
A leafy promenade tracing Tarragona's massive 3rd-century-BC ramparts, where cyclopean stone blocks and watchtowers reveal the oldest Roman construction outside Italy.
Circ Romà and Praetorium Tower
Wander eerie vaulted tunnels beneath the medieval city where Roman chariots once thundered, then climb the Praetorium tower for panoramic rooftop-and-sea views.
Part Alta (Old Town)
Tarragona's honey-stoned upper town tangles medieval lanes, tapas-filled plazas and Roman remnants inside ancient walls, most atmospheric around lively Plaça de la Font.
Museu Nacional Arqueològic de Tarragona
Spain's premier collection of Roman Tarraco treasures, from exquisite mosaics like the Medusa head to statues, coins and everyday objects of imperial Hispania.
Local Forum (Fòrum de la Colònia)
Tucked into a residential quarter, these evocative columned ruins mark the judicial and commercial heart of the Roman colony, quieter than Tarragona's headline sites.
El Serrallo Fishing Quarter
Tarragona's salty maritime soul, where colourful fishermen's houses line the marina and evening auctions supply the seafood restaurants along the harbourfront promenade.

train.note: No international trains stop here. Tarragona has two stations: the central one on the coastal line with Regional and Euromed services to Barcelona in about 1h15, and Camp de Tarragona high-speed station some 10 km inland, where AVE trains reach Barcelona in 35 minutes and Madrid in 2h30. Check which station your ticket names - a shuttle bus links Camp de Tarragona with the city. Booking opens around 60 days ahead.

bus.note: The bus station is near Plaça Imperial Tàrraco. ALSA (https://www.alsa.com/en) and Plana run to Barcelona, Reus, Salou and PortAventura; most European coaches route through Barcelona, an hour up the coast.

ferry.note: Tarragona's port is a large industrial and cruise harbour with no scheduled passenger ferry service. For sailings to the Balearics, Italy or Morocco, use Barcelona, about an hour north.

half.name: Reus
half.blurb: Reus is Antoni Gaudi's birthplace, with a dedicated Gaudi Centre museum and modernist buildings scattered through the compact old town.

half.name: Salou (PortAventura World)
half.blurb: Salou's PortAventura World theme park has roller coasters and water rides, plus long sandy beaches along the Costa Daurada.

half.name: Sitges
half.blurb: Sitges is a beach town north of Tarragona with a whitewashed old quarter, seafront promenade and Modernist-era mansions.

half.name: Montblanc
half.blurb: Montblanc is a walled medieval town with intact stone ramparts, Gothic churches and narrow lanes near the Poblet monastery.

half.name: Royal Abbey of Poblet
half.blurb: The Royal Abbey of Santa Maria de Poblet is a fortified Cistercian monastery and UNESCO site holding royal tombs.
